title: The breast and axillary drainage
summary: Where a lump goes, and why the arm swells afterwards.

steps.title: Where it sits
steps.text:
The breast lies in the superficial fascia over pectoralis major and serratus anterior, from the second to the sixth rib and from the sternum to the mid-axillary line, with an axillary tail of Spence running up into the axilla through a gap in the deep fascia.

Fibrous suspensory ligaments of Cooper run from the skin to the deep fascia; when a tumour drags on them the skin dimples, and lymphoedema between them gives peau d'orange.

check.q: Over which ribs does the breast lie, and what is the axillary tail?
check.a: Ribs 2 to 6; the axillary tail of Spence extends into the axilla through the deep fascia.

steps.title: Blood supply
steps.text: Mainly perforating branches of the internal thoracic artery medially, with lateral thoracic and thoracoacromial branches from the axillary artery laterally, and the posterior intercostals behind. Venous drainage follows, and the connection to the internal thoracic and azygos veins and to the vertebral venous plexus explains metastasis to the vertebrae, lungs and brain.

steps.title: Lymphatic drainage
steps.text: About 75% drains to the axillary nodes, and the rest medially to the parasternal (internal thoracic) nodes – which is why a medial tumour can spread across the midline and to the other breast. The axillary nodes are staged in three levels by their relation to pectoralis minor: level I lateral, level II behind, level III medial.

check.q: What proportion of breast lymph drains to the axilla?
check.a: About 75%; most of the rest goes to the internal thoracic (parasternal) nodes.

steps.title: What is at risk in axillary surgery
steps.text:
Three nerves and one vein lie in the axilla and are looked for by name during clearance: the long thoracic nerve on serratus anterior (winged scapula), the thoracodorsal nerve to latissimus dorsi, the intercostobrachial nerve crossing the axilla (numbness of the inner upper arm) and the axillary vein.

Removing the nodes removes the drainage, hence lymphoedema of the arm.

check.q: Which two nerves are at risk during axillary clearance, and what does each injury cause?
check.a: Long thoracic nerve — winged scapula; thoracodorsal nerve — weak latissimus dorsi.

steps.title: First in the drainage route is not a fixed node number
steps.text:
A sentinel node is one of the first nodes receiving lymph from a particular tissue region or tumour. The term describes a position along a drainage route, not a fixed anatomical node present in exactly the same place in everyone.

Axillary levels I, II and III instead describe where nodes lie relative to pectoralis minor. Most breast lymph reaches the axilla, but routes vary and some reach parasternal nodes. A sentinel node is identified by the actual drainage pathway; its name does not make it synonymous with all level I nodes.

check.q: Does sentinel mean the same thing as axillary level I?
check.a: No. Sentinel describes the first node or nodes on a specific drainage route; level I is a positional category.

steps.title: Why the breast moves over the chest wall
steps.text:
A layer of loose connective tissue in the retromammary plane separates much of the breast from the deep fascia over pectoralis major. It allows the breast to move relative to the underlying muscle and chest wall.

Within the breast, suspensory ligaments connect skin to deeper fascia and organise its support. Tethering of these internal supports can pull on the skin, while involvement of the deeper plane can reduce mobility over the muscle. These are different anatomical relationships, even though both may alter how the breast moves during examination.

check.q: Which plane normally allows the breast to move over pectoralis major?
check.a: The loose connective tissue of the retromammary plane, superficial to the pectoral fascia.

objectives: Describe the extent and structure of the breast
Trace its lymphatic drainage and name the nodal levels
Explain skin dimpling and peau d'orange
Distinguish a sentinel lymph node from an anatomical axillary level and relate breast mobility to the retromammary plane
takeaways: About 75% of lymph drains to the axillary nodes, the rest to internal thoracic nodes.
Suspensory ligaments tether the skin — tumour traction dimples it.
Axillary clearance risks lymphoedema and the long thoracic and thoracodorsal nerves.
Sentinel identifies the first node or nodes on a drainage route; axillary levels describe position relative to pectoralis minor. The retromammary plane permits breast mobility.

title: The autonomic nervous system
summary: Two outflows, where their ganglia sit, and why referred pain works the way it does.

steps.title: Two outflows
steps.text:
Sympathetic: thoracolumbar, T1–L2. Short preganglionic fibres to a ganglion near the cord, long postganglionic fibres to the target.
Parasympathetic: craniosacral – cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X, plus S2–S4. Long preganglionic fibres to a ganglion on or in the organ, short postganglionic fibres.

Spinal autonomic outflow leaves through ventral roots; cranial parasympathetic fibres leave in their cranial nerves. Preganglionic sympathetic fibres enter the chain through white rami; postganglionic fibres returning to spinal nerves use grey rami.

check.q: Where do the two autonomic outflows leave the central nervous system?
check.a: Sympathetic from T1–L2; parasympathetic from cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X and from S2–S4.

steps.title: The sympathetic chain
steps.text:
A chain of ganglia runs the length of the vertebral column on each side. In the neck there are three: superior, middle and the stellate (cervicothoracic) ganglion, which lies against the neck of the first rib.

Damage to the sympathetic supply to the head – a Pancoast tumour, a carotid dissection, a neck injury – gives Horner syndrome: partial ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis on that side.

check.q: Where do sympathetic ganglia lie compared with parasympathetic ones?
check.a: Sympathetic ganglia lie close to the cord in the chain or as prevertebral ganglia; parasympathetic ganglia lie in or near the target organ.

steps.title: The vagus
steps.text:
The vagus carries parasympathetic supply to everything from the pharynx to the transverse colon, plus most of the visceral afferents that never reach consciousness. Below the left colic flexure the parasympathetic supply comes instead from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4).

That watershed – the junction of midgut and hindgut – is also where the blood supply and the referred pain change.

check.q: How far along the gut does the vagus supply?
check.a: To the junction of the proximal two thirds and distal third of the transverse colon.

steps.title: Referred pain
steps.text:
Visceral pain fibres run back with the sympathetics to the spinal segment that supplied the organ in the embryo, and the brain misattributes them to the dermatome of that segment.

Heart (T1–T4): chest, left arm, jaw. Gallbladder (T7–T9): epigastrium and right scapula. Ureter (T11–L2): loin to groin. Diaphragm (C3–C5, phrenic): shoulder tip. Appendix (T10): the umbilicus, until the parietal peritoneum is involved.

check.q: Why is cardiac pain felt in the left arm and jaw?
check.a: Cardiac afferents enter at T1–T4, the same segments as the skin of the arm and the upper chest.

steps.title: White in at some levels, grey out at all
steps.text:
White rami communicantes carry mainly myelinated preganglionic sympathetic fibres into the chain at the thoracolumbar outflow, usually T1-L2. Once inside, a fibre can synapse at that level, travel up or down before synapsing, or pass through towards a prevertebral ganglion.

Grey rami return unmyelinated postganglionic fibres to spinal nerves throughout the column. This lets cervical and sacral nerves carry sympathetic fibres to blood vessels, sweat glands and arrector pili despite having no local white ramus. Distribution can extend much farther than the spinal levels where the preganglionic cells originate.

check.q: How can a cervical spinal nerve carry sympathetic fibres when there is no cervical white ramus?
check.a: Preganglionic fibres ascend in the sympathetic chain, synapse in a cervical ganglion, and postganglionic fibres return through a grey ramus.

steps.title: The ganglion is the relay
steps.text:
Most autonomic efferent pathways use a preganglionic neurone with its cell body in the CNS and a postganglionic neurone in a peripheral ganglion. Parasympathetic ganglia tend to lie near or within the target organ; sympathetic ganglia lie in the chain or in prevertebral groups.

A somatic motor pathway to skeletal muscle instead uses one lower motor neurone from the CNS to the neuromuscular junction. The adrenal medulla is a useful autonomic exception: preganglionic sympathetic fibres activate chromaffin cells, modified postganglionic cells that release catecholamines into blood.

check.q: What replaces the usual postganglionic axon-to-organ connection in the adrenal medulla?
check.a: Chromaffin cells release catecholamines into the circulation after preganglionic sympathetic stimulation.

objectives: Contrast the sympathetic and parasympathetic outflows anatomically
Say where the ganglia of each lie and why that matters
Explain referred visceral pain in terms of afferent pathways
Explain why white rami are limited to thoracolumbar levels while grey rami occur throughout the sympathetic chain
takeaways: Sympathetic outflow is thoracolumbar (T1–L2) with ganglia near the cord; parasympathetic is craniosacral with ganglia in the organ wall.
Parasympathetic supply comes from cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X and from S2–S4.
Visceral pain is referred to the dermatome of the segment the afferents enter.
White rami bring preganglionic fibres into the chain at T1-L2; grey rami return postganglionic fibres to spinal nerves at all levels.

title: Lymphatic drainage
summary: Where lymph goes, and what a big node is telling you.

steps.title: Two ducts
steps.text:
The thoracic duct begins at the cisterna chyli in front of L1/L2, passes through the aortic hiatus, crosses to the left at about T5 and empties into the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins. It drains everything below the diaphragm and the left side above it.

The right lymphatic duct drains only the right head, neck, arm and right thorax.

check.q: Which parts of the body does the right lymphatic duct drain?
check.a: The right side of the head and neck, the right upper limb and the right side of the thorax.

steps.title: Virchow's node
steps.text: Because the thoracic duct ends in the left venous angle, a tumour that has seeded the duct can enlarge the left supraclavicular node. A hard, fixed node there – Troisier's sign – points to an abdominal primary, classically gastric, but also pancreatic, testicular or ovarian.

check.q: What does an enlarged left supraclavicular node suggest?
check.a: Abdominal malignancy, classically gastric — Virchow's node, at the end of the thoracic duct.

steps.title: Watersheds that decide the operation
steps.text:
The pectinate line in the anal canal: above it lymph goes to internal iliac nodes, below it to superficial inguinal nodes – and the blood supply, venous drainage, epithelium and innervation all change there too.

The testis descended from the abdomen, so it drains to para-aortic nodes, while the scrotal skin drains to the inguinal nodes: a testicular tumour therefore does not present with an inguinal node.

check.q: Why does the lymph drainage of the testis differ from that of the scrotum?
check.a: The testis descends from the posterior abdominal wall and keeps its para-aortic drainage; the scrotal skin is perineal and drains to inguinal nodes.

steps.title: A one-way entrance from the tissue
steps.text:
Initial lymphatic capillaries begin blindly in tissues. Their overlapping endothelial edges act as small entry flaps: rising interstitial pressure helps open them, admitting fluid and proteins that have left the blood microcirculation.

Larger collecting lymphatics have valves and smooth muscle that support forward movement. Skeletal muscle activity and breathing also help drive flow towards the venous angles. There is no single lymphatic heart. When lymphatic drainage is impaired, protein-rich fluid can accumulate in tissues despite the presence of intact arteries and veins.

check.q: Why can lymphatic obstruction cause swelling even if the main veins are open?
check.a: Lymphatics have a separate role returning interstitial fluid and proteins; patent veins do not replace that drainage.

steps.title: A node filters what has already left the blood
steps.text:
Lymph nodes filter lymph arriving from tissues through afferent lymphatic vessels. Immune cells sample material carried with that fluid before it leaves through efferent vessels and continues towards larger collecting trunks.

The spleen performs surveillance of blood rather than acting as a node on an afferent lymphatic route. Both are lymphoid organs, but they encounter material delivered by different circulations. When considering where an immune response or metastatic deposit may appear first, begin with the fluid pathway serving the tissue.

check.q: Which organ samples material arriving mainly in blood rather than afferent lymph: a lymph node or the spleen?
check.a: The spleen; lymph nodes sample lymph arriving from tissues.

objectives: Describe the general plan of lymphatic drainage
Say what the thoracic duct drains and where it ends
Interpret an enlarged node by its drainage field
Explain how lymph enters blind-ended capillaries and returns to veins without a central pump
takeaways: The thoracic duct drains everything except the right upper quadrant of the body.
Lymph enters the venous system at the junction of the internal jugular and subclavian veins.
An enlarged node points to its drainage field — Virchow's node points to the abdomen.
Overlapping lymphatic endothelial flaps admit interstitial fluid; valves, vessel-wall contraction, breathing and muscle movement support return to the venous angles.
